'''''Sabal mexicana''''' is a species of [[Arecaceae|palm tree]] that is native to far southern [[North America]].  Common names include '''Rio Grande palmetto''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SAME8|taxon=Sabal mexicana|accessdate=26 October 2015}}</ref> '''Mexican palmetto''', '''Texas palmetto''', '''Texas sabal palm''', '''palmetto cabbage''' and '''palma de mícharos'''.<ref name="Grin"/> The [[specific name (botany)|specific epithet]], ''"mexicana"'', is [[Latin]] for "of [[Mexico]]."<ref name="Riffle">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rL3dHVJ2CZ8C |first=Robert Lee |last=Riffle |author2=Paul Craft  |title=An Encyclopedia of Cultivated Palms |year=2003 |publisher=Timber Press |isbn=978-0-88192-558-6 |pages=446–447}}</ref>

==Description==
Mexican palmetto reaches a height of {{convert|12|-|18|m|ft|abbr=on}}, with a spread of {{convert|3|-|4|m|ft|abbr=on}}. The [[Trunk (botany)|trunk]] reaches {{convert|12|-|15|m|ft|abbr=on}} in length and {{convert|30|cm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter.  The fan-shaped [[frond]]s are {{convert|1.5|-|1.8|m|ft|abbr=on}} wide and attach to {{convert|90|-|120|cm|in|abbr=on}} spineless [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]]s.  [[Raceme|Spikes]] {{convert|1.2|-|1.8|m|ft|abbr=on}} in length yield small [[Plant sexuality|bisexual]] [[flower]]s.<ref name="Timber">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NARcoCeQVPcC |title=Timber Press Pocket Guide to Palms |first=Robert Lee |last=Riffle |publisher=Timber Press |year=2008 |isbn=978-0-88192-776-4 |page=204}}</ref>  The [[drupe]]s<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3PbQaKSDJfUC |title=Landscaping with Native Plants of Texas |first=George Oxford |last=Miller |publisher=Voyageur Press |year=2006 |isbn=978-0-7603-2539-1|page=94}}</ref> are black when ripe and {{convert|12|mm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter.<ref name="Timber"/>

==Range==
The current range of ''S. mexicana'' extends from [[South Texas]] on the [[Gulf Coast]] of the [[United States]] and [[Nayarit]] on the [[Pacific coast|Pacific Coast]], south along both seashores to [[Nicaragua]].<ref name="Grin"/> It is one of the most widespread and common [[Arecaceae|palm trees]] in [[Mexico]], where it is found in the drier lowlands.<ref name="Henderson">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zZ2flHoGLtcC |title=Field Guide to the Palms of the Americas |first=Andrew |last=Henderson |author2=Gloria Galeano |author3=Rodrigo Bernal  |publisher=Princeton University Press |year=1997 |isbn=978-0-691-01600-9 |page=66}}</ref> Some believe that the species may have ranged much further north along the Texas [[Gulf Coast of the United States|Gulf Coast]] and as far inland as [[San Antonio]] at one time. This is supported by observations recorded in the 17th to 19th centuries, the presence of a small, [[Disjunct distribution|disjunct population]] {{convert|200|mi|km|abbr=on}} north of the Lower Rio Grande Valley, and the ease with which cultivated trees have become [[Introduced species|naturalized]] in parts of [[Central Texas]].<ref name="Lockett">{{cite journal |url=http://www.npsot.org/events/FallSymposium/2006/SymposiumProceedings2006_V5.pdf |format=PDF |first=Landon |last=Lockett |title=Sabal Mexicana Palm Trees, Native to San Antonio. And Beyond? |journal=Convergence and Diversity: Native Plants of South Central Texas Symposium Proceedings |publisher=[[Native Plant Society of Texas]] |year=2006 |pages=79–84 |archive-date=2011-06-08 |access-date=2010-01-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110608174807/http://www.npsot.org/events/FallSymposium/2006/SymposiumProceedings2006_V5.pdf }}</ref> ''S. mexicana'' should not be confused with the related and somewhat shorter "Brazoria Palm", a small population of which occurs in southeast Texas, and which is a natural hybrid of ''S. palmetto'' and ''S. minor''.<ref name="S. brazoriensis">{{cite journal|last=Goldman|first=Douglas |author2=Klooster, Griffith |author3=Fay, Chase|title=A preliminary evaluation of the ancestry of a putative Sabal hybrid (Arecaceae:  Coryphoideae), and the description of a new nothospecies, Sabal × brazoriensis|journal=Phytotaxa|date=2011-08-25|volume=27|series=1179|issue=3163|url=http://www.mapress.com/phytotaxa/content/2011/f/p00027p025f.pdf}}</ref>

Naturally occurring ''S. mexicana'' in Texas may be difficult to discern, because this palm is widely planted as an ornamental, and because feral specimens easily become established.  However, at least two populations in Texas have been reported to be purely natural.  The most prominent is found in the 557-acre [[Sabal Palm Sanctuary]] located outside of Brownsville, Texas, along the banks of the Rio Grande.  The second is on a much smaller tract located along the banks of Garcitas Creek, near Vanderbilt, Texas.

==Uses==
Mexican palmetto is grown as an [[Ornamental plant|ornamental]] for its robust, stately form, [[drought]] tolerance, and [[Hardy palms|hardiness]] to [[Hardiness zone#USDA hardiness zones|USDA Zone 8]].<ref name="Floridata">{{cite web |url=http://www.floridata.com/ref/S/saba_mex.cfm |title=#813 Sabal mexicana |publisher=Floridata |access-date=2010-01-08}}</ref> The wood is [[Wood preservation#Naturally rot-resistant woods|resistant]] to [[decomposition]]<ref name="Floridata"/> and [[shipworm]]s, making it desirable for use in [[wharf]] [[Deep foundation|pilings]]<ref name="Lockett"/> and [[fence]] posts.<ref name="Floridata"/> The [[Leaf|leaves]] are used for [[thatching]] and making [[straw hat]]s. The [[drupe]]s and [[Heart of palm|palm hearts]] are eaten.<ref name="Henderson"/>
